can: Write genotypes and gametes, then fill a Punnett square without a slip.
Give a result as a ratio, a percentage or a probability, as asked.
Describe a test cross and read genotypes off a pedigree diagram.

text: Monohybrid crosses, Punnett squares, test crosses and pedigrees

md: One characteristic, one gene, two versions of it. Every genetics question on the paper is the same short move, dressed up in a different animal or plant. Learn the move once and the dressing stops mattering.

text: 1. Six words, and what each one is about

alt: Six rows. Genotype: the two alleles a plant or animal carries, such as BB, Bb or bb. Phenotype: the characteristic you can see, such as a black or a chestnut coat. Homozygous: two alleles the same. Heterozygous: two alleles different. Dominant: shows whenever it is present. Recessive: shows only when both alleles are recessive.

md:
Coat colour in the Shetland pony: **B** gives a black coat and **b** gives a chestnut one.

The **genotype** is the pair of alleles an animal carries — BB, Bb or bb. The **phenotype** is what you can see — black or chestnut.

**Homozygous** means the two alleles are the same (BB or bb). **Heterozygous** means they are different (Bb).

prompt: A pony carries the alleles B and b for coat colour. What one word describes that genotype?
explain: Heterozygous: two different alleles. BB and bb are the homozygous ones.

text: 2. Why one allele can hide the other

alt: Three boxes. The genotype BB gives a black coat and the genotype Bb also gives a black coat, because one B is enough. The genotype bb gives a chestnut coat, because the recessive allele only shows when there is no B.

md:
A **dominant** allele shows in the phenotype whenever it is there. A **recessive** allele shows only when there is no dominant allele to hide it.

So **BB** and **Bb** both give a black coat, and only **bb** gives a chestnut one.

That is why a chestnut animal is easy: its genotype can only be **bb**. A black one is the puzzle, because it could be either of two.

prompt: In Shetland ponys, B gives a black coat and b gives a chestnut coat. What must a pony carry to have a chestnut coat?
explain: Two recessive alleles, written bb. A single B would be enough to make the coat black.

md:
**Step 1 — parents' genotypes.** Read them out of the question, and write them down before anything else.
**Step 2 — gametes.** Split each genotype into its two letters. A gamete carries **one** allele, never two.
**Step 3 — offspring.** Pair every gamete of one parent with every gamete of the other.
**Step 4 — count.** Then answer in whatever form the question asks for.

title: What is not examined here
md: CCEA's genetic diagrams always follow one characteristic, controlled by a single gene with two alleles. Codominance and crosses following two genes at once are not on the specification, so let a video that covers them pass. Sex linkage comes, at Higher, in the next topic.

prompt: A pony has the genotype Bb. What does each of its gametes carry?
options: one allele, either B or b
two alleles the same, BB or bb
answer: one allele, either B or b
explain: One allele each. Meiosis halves the number, so a gamete gets one of the pair — and a gamete written as Bb is the commonest slip in this topic.

title: Worked example: two black ponies, both Bb, are crossed. What is the probability that a foal is chestnut? [3]
md:
**Step 1 — genotypes and gametes.** Both parents are **Bb**, so each makes **B and b** gametes. **[1]**
**Step 2 — fill the square.** Row by row: **BB, Bb, Bb, bb**. **[1]**
**Step 3 — count what was asked for.** chestnut needs **bb**, and 1 box in 4 is bb, so the probability is **25%**. **[1]**

The check: the four boxes must add up to the whole litter, so the two percentages come to 100.

prompt: Two black ponies with genotype Bb are crossed. What percentage of their foals would you expect to be chestnut?
explain: 1 box out of 4 is bb, so 25%. The other 75% show the dominant phenotype.

md:
The square gives you four boxes. The question decides how you report them.

**Ratio** — 3 : 1, with the numbers in the order the question names the phenotypes.
**Percentage** — 75% and 25%.
**Probability** — 1 in 4, or one quarter.

Two traps live here. A **ratio written backwards** loses the mark, and so does a **genotype ratio** (1 : 2 : 1) given where a **phenotype ratio** was asked for.

prompt: A cross gives 3 black foals for every 1 chestnut one. Write that as a phenotype ratio, black to chestnut.
explain: 3 : 1. The order follows the question, so the black number comes first here.

md:
**Higher tier.** A black animal is either **BB** or **Bb**, and you cannot tell by looking. A **test cross** asks it the question.

Cross the unknown with a **chestnut** animal, which can only be **bb**. Then:

• every offspring black → the unknown was **BB**;
• any chestnut offspring at all → the unknown was **Bb**.

prompt: A breeder test-crosses a black pony with a chestnut one and gets one chestnut foal. What does that show about the black parent?
options: nothing can be decided from one foal
explain: The chestnut foal is bb, so it took a b from each parent. The black parent must therefore carry a b, which makes it Bb.

caption: Start with the shaded symbols: every one of them is bb.

md:
**Higher tier.** Squares are males, circles are females, and a shaded symbol shows the recessive phenotype.

Work in this order. **Shaded first**: every shaded symbol is **bb**. **Then the parents of a shaded child**: each gave a b, so a black parent of a chestnut child is **Bb**. **Then anyone with a chestnut parent**: they carry a b too.

Anything left over is "BB or Bb", and saying so is the right answer.

title: The exact relationship, and the word in bold
md: The report notes two habits that cost marks: 'parent' written where 'father' was wanted, and half a phenotype, the condition without male or female, where a bold word asked for all of it. Read any bold word twice.

prompt: On the pedigree of Labrador retrievers shown, individual 1 is black and has a chocolate puppy. What one word describes individual 1's genotype?
explain: Heterozygous, written Bb. The chocolate puppy is bb and took one b from each parent, so individual 1 must carry a b even though it does not show.

md: This is a late question worth about seven to eleven marks, opened by a pedigree diagram or by a described cross. The first mark is almost always a genotype; the last is a ratio, a percentage or a test cross described in full. A wrong parental genotype loses that mark but the square drawn correctly from it still earns its own, so show the square. Stuck? Write the parents' letters and split them.
